lesson.title: As One Goes Up, the Other Goes Down: Negative Correlation
lesson.summary: Negative correlation describes a relationship where increases in one variable tend to accompany decreases in another, visible on a scatterplot as a downward drift from left to right.
lesson.body:
You already know from correlation that a scatterplot can reveal whether two quantities tend to move together, and if so, in which direction. Positive correlation happens when both variables rise together. Negative correlation is its mirror image: as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease. On a scatterplot, this shows up as a cloud of points that drifts downward as you move from left to right.

Think about outdoor temperature and cups of hot chocolate sold at a campus coffee cart. As the temperature climbs, fewer people want a hot drink, so sales tend to fall. As the temperature drops, more people crave something warm, so sales tend to rise. These two quantities move in opposite directions, which is exactly what negative correlation means.

Worked example. Suppose the coffee cart records temperature and cups sold on five different days:

Temperature (F): 30, 40, 50, 60, 70
Cups sold: 50, 40, 32, 22, 10

Read the pattern from left to right: as temperature rises by 10 degrees each time, cups sold falls, first by 10, then by 8, then by 10, then by 12. The exact drop is not identical every time, real data rarely is that tidy, but the direction is unmistakable: every increase in temperature comes with a decrease in cups sold. If you plotted these five points, they would trend down and to the right, the visual signature of negative correlation.

Correlation also has strength, not just direction. If the points fall close to a clean downward line, the negative correlation is strong. If they still trend downward but are more spread out, the negative correlation is weaker. The hot chocolate data above is a fairly strong negative correlation because the downward drift is consistent even though the drops vary slightly.

One caution worth remembering: a negative correlation tells you two variables tend to move in opposite directions, it does not automatically tell you why. Colder weather does not force anyone to buy hot chocolate, it just makes people more likely to want it. Whenever you spot a correlation, positive or negative, treat it as a pattern to investigate, not proof of a cause.
